claim: Efficient information transfer in neural networks depends crucially upon the balance between excitation and inhibition (E/I-Balance).
source: Emerging evidence suggests that efficient information transfer in neural networks depends crucially upon the balance between excitation and inhibition (E/I-Balance) (Shu et al., 2003; Haider et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shu et al., 2003 and Haider et al., 2006.

claim: A shift in E/I-balance towards elevated excitability has been recently implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia.
source: A shift in E/I-balance towards elevated excitability has been recently implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia (ScZ) (Driesen et al., 2013; Lisman, 2012; Murray et al., 2014; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Driesen et al., 2013; Lisman, 2012; Murray et al., 2014; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2012.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic interneurons are of particular interest in the maintenance of E/I-balance.
source: Among the circuit mechanisms that are involved in the maintenance of E/I-balance, parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic interneurons are of particular interest (Xue et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Xue et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of pyramidal cell activity by PV+ interneurons regulates the output of cell-assemblies and leads to rhythmic fluctuations in excitability or neural oscillations.
source: as inhibition of pyramidal cell activity regulates the output of cell-assemblies and leads to rhythmic fluctuations in excitability or neural oscillations (Sohal et al., 2009; Kopell and LeMasson, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sohal et al., 2009 and Kopell and LeMasson, 1994.

claim: AMPA- and NMDA-R-mediated activation of PV+ interneurons is essential for the generation of oscillatory activity, especially at gamma-band (30–90 Hz) frequencies.
source: Moreover, there is consistent evidence that α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA)- and N-methyl-D-aspartate Receptor (NMDA-R)-mediated activation of PV+ interneurons is essential for the generation of oscillatory activity (Carlén et al., 2012; Fuchs et al., 2007), especially at gamma-band (30–90 Hz) frequencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carlén et al., 2012 and Fuchs et al., 2007.

claim: In schizophrenia, converging evidence from genetics, post-mortem data and brain imaging have supported the possibility that E/I-balance is disrupted.
source: In ScZ, converging evidence from genetics (Pocklington et al., 2015), post-mortem data (Lewis et al., 2012) and brain imaging (Kegeles et al., 2012) have supported the possibility that E/I-balance is disrupted
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pocklington et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2012; and Kegeles et al., 2012.

claim: Task-related gamma-band oscillations are reduced in schizophrenia.
source: which is consistent with observations from electro/magnetoencephalographical (EEG/MEG)-data that task-related, gamma-band oscillations are reduced (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010.

claim: A shift in E/I-balance in schizophrenia towards increased excitability-levels predicts an increase in spontaneous gamma-band activity.
source: One central prediction for a shift in E/I-balance in ScZ towards increased excitability-levels is an increase in spontaneous gamma-band activity
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the E/I-balance hypothesis.

claim: Pre-clinical data show that transient increases in excitability are associated with enhanced occurrence of gamma-band power.
source: and a wealth of evidence from pre-clinical (Yizhar et al., 2011; Kocsis, 2012; Pinault, 2008) as well as data in healthy controls following NMDA-R hypofunctioning (Rivolta et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2015) highlight that transient increases in excitability are associated with enhanced occurrence of gamma-band power.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Yizhar et al., 2011; Kocsis, 2012; Pinault, 2008; Rivolta et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2015.

claim: NMDA-R antagonists increase spontaneous gamma-band activity in both human and pre-clinical research.
source: For example, NMDA-R antagonists have been show to increase spontaneous gamma-band activity in both human (Rivolta et al., 2015) and pre-clinical research (Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rivolta et al., 2015 and Saunders et al., 2012.

claim: MRS studies show a consistent finding of an elevation of Glutamate-levels across illness-stages in schizophrenia.
source: A consistent finding is an elevation of Glutamate-levels across illness-stages in ScZ (Merritt et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Merritt et al., 2016.

claim: The evidence for changes in GABA-levels in schizophrenia is less consistent.
source: while the evidence for changes in GABA-levels is less consistent (Egerton et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Egerton et al., 2017.

claim: MEG is characterized by an improved signal-to-noise ratio for measurements of high-frequency oscillations compared to EEG.
source: MEG is characterized by an improved signal-to-noise ratio for measurements of high-frequency oscillations compared to EEG (Muthukumaraswamy and Singh, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Muthukumaraswamy and Singh, 2013.

claim: The signatures of fMRI resting-state networks during early stage psychosis, but not in chronic schizophrenia, resemble the acute effects of NMDA-R hypofunctioning.
source: Previous data highlighted that the signatures of fMRI resting-state networks during early stage psychosis, but not in chronic ScZ, resemble the acute effects of NMDA-R hypofunctioning (Anticevic et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Anticevic et al., 2015.

claim: Glutamatergic neurotransmission is increased in younger schizophrenia patients.
source: In addition, there is evidence that glutamatergic neurotransmission is increased in younger ScZ-patients (Marsman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marsman et al., 2013.

claim: The chronic schizophrenia group was significantly older than the control participants.
source: The chronic ScZ-group was significantly older than the control participants.
evidence: This is stated in the demographic and clinical characteristics section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: There were significantly more females in the CHR group than in the FEP and chronic schizophrenia groups.
source: There were also significantly more females in the CHR than in the FEP and chronic ScZ-groups.
evidence: This is stated in the demographic and clinical characteristics section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: FEP-patients were characterized by higher ratings on the Excitation, Cognitive, Positive and Depression PANSS subscales and total PANSS-scores than the chronic schizophrenia group.
source: FEP-patients were characterized by higher ratings on the Excitation, Cognitive, Positive and Depression PANSS subscales and total PANSS-scores than the chronic ScZ group.
evidence: This is stated in the demographic and clinical characteristics section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Neurocognitive data showed an overall increase in severity and range of cognitive deficits across the course of illness.
source: Neurocognitive data showed an overall increase in severity and range of cognitive deficits across the course of illness.
evidence: This is stated in the demographic and clinical characteristics section and supported by BACS data in Table 1.

claim: FEP-patients showed significantly decreased prefrontal cortex low gamma-band activity.
source: FEP-patients showed significantly decreased prefrontal cortex low gamma-band activity (−2.15 < t(56)<−3.79, 0.002 < p < 0.006; see Table 2 for specific locations)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: FEP-patients showed increased occipital cortex low gamma-band activity.
source: while occipital cortex activity was increased (2.82 < t(56)<3.80, 0.002 < p < 0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: Chronic schizophrenia patients showed widespread decreased low gamma-band activity in frontal, temporal and sensorimotor areas.
source: In contrast, chronic ScZ patients showed widespread decreased low gamma-band activity in frontal, temporal and sensorimotor areas (−2.35 < t(69)<−4.24, 0.002 < p < 0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: A significant increase in high gamma-band power was found in both midfrontal and posterior-occipital and angular gyrus in CHR-participants.
source: A significant increase in high gamma-band power was found in both midfrontal and posterior-occipital and angular gyrus in CHR-participants (2.40 < t(134)<2.74, 0.002 < p < 0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: In FEP patients, changes in high gamma-band power showed strong increases in posterior regions.
source: In FEP and ScZ-patients, changes in high gamma-band power were comparable to those seen at lower gamma-band frequencies, with strong increases in posterior regions for the FEP-group (2.48 < t(56)<4.08, 0.002 < p < 0.006)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: FEP patients showed moderate decreases in frontal high gamma-band power.
source: and moderate decreases in frontal high gamma-band power in both FEP (−2.42 < t(56)<−3.26, 0.002 < p < 0.006)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: Chronic schizophrenia patients showed moderate decreases in frontal high gamma-band power.
source: and moderate decreases in frontal high gamma-band power in both FEP (−2.42 < t(56)<−3.26, 0.002 < p < 0.006) and chronic SCZ-patients (−2.40 < t(69)<−3.56, 0.002 < p < 0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: Different CHR-groups are associated with differential risks for psychosis, with CHR-participants meeting both CAARMS/SPI-A criteria having the highest risk for the development of psychosis followed by CAARMS and SPI-A only groups.
source: Previous data (Schultze-Lutter et al., 2014) indicated that different CHR-groups are associated with differential risks for psychosis, with CHR-participants meeting both CAARMS/SPI-A criteria having the highest risk for the development of psychosis followed by CAARMs and SPI-A only groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schultze-Lutter et al., 2014.

claim: The combined SPI-A/CAARMS group was characterized by increased frontal and posterior cortex 64–90 Hz power.
source: The combined SPI-A/CAARMS group was characterized by increased frontal and posterior cortex 64–90 Hz power (Figure 2: 2.16 < t(80)<3.43, 0.002 < p < 0.006)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Increased high gamma-band power was not present in the SPI-A only group.
source: which was not present in the SPI-A only group.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: CHR-participants who only met CAARMS criteria showed moderately increased middle frontal and occipital cortex high gamma-band power.
source: CHR-participants who only met CAARMS criteria showed moderately increased middle frontal and occipital cortex high gamma-band power (Figure 2: t(75) = 2.67, p=0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The increase in upregulated occipital cortex high gamma-band activity in the combined SPI-A/CAARMS groups showed an overlap with the pattern observed in the FEP-group.
source: Interestingly, the increase in upregulated occipital cortex high gamma-band activity in the combined SPI-A/CAARMS groups showed an overlap with the pattern observed in the FEP-group (Figure 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of MEG data patterns and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Upregulated occipital cortex high gamma-band activity was not present in chronic schizophrenia patients.
source: but was not present in chronic ScZ-patients
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: Down-regulated gamma-band power in frontal, temporal and sensorimotor regions was only seen in patients with schizophrenia but not in CHR-participants.
source: whereas the down-regulated gamma-band power in frontal, temporal and sensorimotor regions was only seen in patients with ScZ but not in CHR-participants.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: All reported group-specific gamma-band power effects were broadband in nature.
source: Statistical analyses of these data confirmed that all reported group-specific gamma-band power effects were broadband in nature (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both total CAARMS and composite BACS scores correlated with gamma-band power, especially in the 64 – 90 Hz frequency range, in the CHR-group.
source: Both total CAARMS and composite BACS scores correlated with gamma-band power, especially in the 64 – 90 Hz frequency range, in the CHR-group
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of MEG and clinical data presented in the Results section.

claim: Increases in gamma-band activity in the CHR-group were related to neurocognitive deficits and elevated psychotic symptoms.
source: suggesting that increases in gamma-band activity were related to neurocognitive deficits and elevated psychotic symptoms.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of MEG and clinical data presented in the Results section.

claim: In the FEP-group, similar relationships between gamma-band power and clinical measures were observed for posterior areas, while frontal and central regions showed an opposite relationship.
source: Similar relationships were observed for the FEP-group for posterior areas, while frontal and central regions showed an opposite relationship.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of MEG and clinical data presented in the Results section.

claim: In the chronic schizophrenia group, BACS and PANSS-scores were mostly correlated with a reduction of gamma-band power, especially in the lower gamma-band range.
source: In the chronic ScZ-group, BACS and PANSS-scores were mostly correlated with a reduction of gamma-band power, especially in the lower gamma-band range.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of MEG and clinical data presented in the Results section.

claim: Across groups, modest correlations were observed between age and sex.
source: Across groups, modest correlations were observed between age and sex.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: In the chronic schizophrenia group, widespread correlations at both low and high gamma-band ranges were observed with age.
source: In the chronic ScZ-group, widespread correlations at both low and high gamma-band ranges were observed with age.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: The CHR-group showed significantly higher excitatory Glx concentrations in right middle occipital gyrus compared to controls.
source: Results from one-way repeated-measures ANOVAs showed that, compared to controls, the CHR-group showed significantly higher excitatory Glx concentrations in right middle occipital gyrus (F(1,102) = 4.3, p=0.041, Welch-t = 5.9, p=0.017, LSD corrected)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MRS data presented in the Results section.

claim: The CHR-group showed no changes in GABA concentrations compared to controls.
source: in the absence of changes in GABA concentrations (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MRS data and reference to Figure 5.

claim: CHR-participants showed a significantly increased Glx/GABA ratio compared to controls.
source: The imbalance in concentrations between excitatory Glx and inhibitory GABA concentrations in CHR-participants was evident also in a significantly increased Glx/GABA ratio (F(1,102) = 4.5, p=0.037, Welch-t(102)=5.8, p=0.018, LSD corrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of MRS data presented in the Results section.

claim: Changes in Glx and Glx/GABA ratio correlated significantly with increased right and left calcarine and right middle occipital gyrus high gamma-band power.
source: These analyses showed that changes in Glx and Glx/GABA ratio correlated significantly (p<0.05, uncorrected) with increased right and left calcarine and right middle occipital gyrus high gamma-band power (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of MRS and MEG data and reference to Figure 5.

claim: Increased high gamma-band power correlated significantly with decreased calcarine fissure GABA concentrations.
source: In addition, increased high gamma-band power correlated significantly with decreased calcarine fissure GABA concentrations as well as with increased Glx/GABA ratio (p<0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of MRS and MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: Increased high gamma-band power correlated significantly with increased Glx/GABA ratio.
source: In addition, increased high gamma-band power correlated significantly with decreased calcarine fissure GABA concentrations as well as with increased Glx/GABA ratio (p<0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of MRS and MEG data presented in the Results section.

claim: CHR-participants were characterized by distinct patterns of resting-state gamma-band power compared to FEP and chronic schizophrenia groups.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we observed distinct patterns of resting-state gamma-band power in CHR-, FEP- and chronic ScZ-groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by the MEG data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: CHR-participants were characterized by increased gamma-band power compared to both FEP and chronic schizophrenia in a network including frontal and right temporal structures.
source: Specifically, CHR-participants were characterized by increased gamma-band power compared to both FEP and chronic ScZ in a network including frontal and right temporal structures.
evidence: The claim is supported by the MEG data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: FEP-patients showed largely reduced 30–90 Hz power over frontal, central and temporal areas.
source: FEP-patients showed largely reduced 30–90 Hz power over frontal, central and temporal areas
evidence: The claim is supported by the MEG data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: FEP-patients showed additional increases in visual areas not observed in the chronic schizophrenia group.
source: but also showed additional increases in visual areas not observed in the chronic ScZ-group.
evidence: The claim is supported by the MEG data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: The changes observed in gamma-band power across illness stages covered the entire 30–90 Hz frequency range, except for the CHR group where the increases in spectral power selectively involved the 64–90 Hz frequency band.
source: Importantly, the changes observed in gamma-band power across illness stages covered the entire 30–90 Hz frequency range, except for the CHR group where the increases in spectral power selectively involved the 64–90 Hz frequency band
evidence: The claim is supported by the MEG data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: High gamma-band activity may constitute a marker for psychosis-risk.
source: suggesting that high gamma-band activity may constitute a marker for psychosis-risk.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective involvement of 64–90 Hz frequency band in CHR participants.

claim: The pattern of spectral changes is distinct from activity associated with an oscillatory process observed during task-contexts.
source: Overall, the pattern of spectral changes is distinct from activity associated with an oscillatory process observed during task-contexts (Hoogenboom et al., 2006; Fries et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoogenboom et al., 2006 and Fries et al., 2008.

claim: A circumscribed modulation within a particular frequency is considered to be the hallmark of an oscillation.
source: whereby a circumscribed modulation within a particular frequency is considered to be the hallmark of an oscillation.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about oscillatory processes.

claim: The broad-band modulation observed in the data is compatible with the effects of impaired NMDA-R on PV+ cells.
source: The broad-band modulation observed in our data is compatible with the effects of impaired NMDA-R on PV+ cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and known mechanisms.

claim: Reduced NMDA-R neurotransmission on PV+ interneurons is associated with increased broad-band gamma-band power at rest.
source: Carlén et al. (2012) showed that reduced NMDA-R neurotransmission on PV+ interneurons is associated with increased broad-band gamma-band power at rest
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Carlén et al., 2012.

claim: The ability to generate gamma-band oscillations after optogenetic drive of PV-interneurons was reduced in conditions of reduced NMDA-R neurotransmission.
source: while the ability to generate gamma-band oscillations after optogenetic drive of PV-interneurons was reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Carlén et al., 2012.

claim: The current data replicate the large body of evidence for impaired generation of task-related, band-limited gamma-band oscillations in schizophrenia.
source: These data thus also replicate the large body of evidence for impaired generation of task-related, band-limited gamma-band oscillations in ScZ (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010; Thuné et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010 and Thuné et al., 2016.

claim: Impaired E/I-balance is crucial for the explanation for alterations in both resting-state as well as task-related gamma-band activity in schizophrenia.
source: highlighting the crucial importance of impaired E/I-balance for the explanation for alterations in both resting-state as well as task-related gamma-band activity in ScZ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and known mechanisms.

claim: Elevated excitation due to NMDA-R hypofunctioning has been implicated as a possible mechanism for the emergence of psychosis.
source: Elevated excitation due to NMDA-R hypofunctioning has been implicated as a possible mechanism for the emergence of psychosis (Schobel et al., 2013)

claim: NMDA-R hypofunctioning could transiently lead to elevated high-frequency activity.

claim: Psychosis-risk is intimately related to elevated glutamatergic neurotransmission.
source: highlighting that psychosis-risk is intimately related to elevated glutamatergic neurotransmission.

source: and findings in FEP (Kahn and Sommer, 2015).

claim: Increased Glx-levels extend into visual cortex.

claim: E/I-balance is fundamental for shaping information transmission of large-scale networks during normal brain functioning.
source: During normal brain functioning, E/I-balance is fundamental for shaping information transmission of large-scale networks (Yizhar et al., 2011; Saunders et al., 2012).

claim: The findings are potentially consistent with the NMDA-R hypofunctioning model of psychosis.
source: and are potentially consistent with the NMDA-R hypofunctioning model of psychosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and existing models.

claim: The findings have implications for current pathophysiological theories emphasizing a shift towards increased excitation in the early stage of schizophrenia.
source: These findings have implications for current pathophysiological theories emphasizing a shift towards increased excitation in the early stage of ScZ, with possible implications for the development of treatments and biomarkers for early detection and diagnosis.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Future studies should investigate the possibility of utilizing resting-state gamma-band power as spectral fingerprints to predict onset of psychosis as well as treatment outcomes.
source: Accordingly, future studies should investigate the possibility of utilizing resting-state gamma-band power as spectral fingerprints (Siegel et al., 2012) to predict onset of psychosis as well as treatment outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions, supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2012.

claim: A total of n = 22 participants' data were excluded due to excessive muscle and movement artefacts.
source: A total of n = 22 participants' data were excluded due to excessive muscle and movement artefacts (10 CHR, 3 FEP, 4 chronic ScZ and 5 controls).
evidence: This is a statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: CHR-participants were recruited from NHS-services and the general population.
source: CHR-participants were recruited from NHS-services and the general population.
evidence: This is a statement about participant recruitment.

claim: CHR-criteria were established through the CAARMS Interview for the assessment of attenuated psychotic symptoms and the COGDIS/COPER items of the SPI-A.
source: CHR-criteria were established through the Comprehensive Assessment of At Risk Mental States (CAARMS) Interview (Yung et al., 2005) for the assessment of attenuated psychotic symptoms and the Cognitive Disturbances and Cognitive-Perceptive Basic Symptoms (COGDIS/COPER) items of the Schizophrenia Proneness Instrument, Adult version (SPI-A) (Schultze-Lutter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the assessment methods used, supported by citations to Yung et al., 2005 and Schultze-Lutter et al., 2007.

claim: Basic symptoms describe a range of self-experienced cognitive and perceptual abnormalities that are predictive for the development of schizophrenia.
source: Basic symptoms describe a range of self-experienced cognitive and perceptual abnormalities that are predictive for the development of ScZ (Klosterkötter et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klosterkötter et al., 2001.

claim: CHR-participants were excluded for current or past diagnosis with Axis I psychotic disorders, including affective psychoses, as determined by the SCID.
source: CHR-participants were excluded for current or past diagnosis with Axis I psychotic disorders, including affective psychoses, as determined by the Structured Clinical Interview for the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-IV (SCID).
evidence: This is a statement about exclusion criteria.

claim: Other co-morbid Axis I diagnoses, such as mood or anxiety disorders, were not exclusionary for CHR-participants.
source: Other co-morbid Axis I diagnoses, such as mood or anxiety disorders, were not exclusionary
evidence: This is a statement about inclusion criteria.

claim: All CHR-participants were between 16 – 35 years of age.
source: and all participants were between 16 – 35 years of age
evidence: This is a statement about inclusion criteria.

claim: FEP schizophrenia patients were recruited from the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, University of Cologne.
source: FEP ScZ-patients were recruited from the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, University of Cologne
evidence: This is a statement about participant recruitment.

claim: Chronic schizophrenia patients were recruited from the Department of Psychiatry, Psychosomatics and Psychotherapy, Goethe University Frankfurt.
source: and chronic ScZ patients from the Department of Psychiatry, Psychosomatics and Psychotherapy, Goethe University Frankfurt.
evidence: This is a statement about participant recruitment.

claim: Current psychopathology was examined with the PANSS.
source: Current psychopathology was examined with the Positive and Negative Symptom Scale (PANSS) (Kay et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a statement about the assessment methods used, supported by citation to Kay et al., 1987.

claim: Control participants were screened for psychopathology with the SCID and/or the MINI-SCID interview.
source: Control participants were screened for psychopathology with the SCID and/or the MINI-SCID interview (Sheehan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about the assessment methods used, supported by citation to Sheehan et al., 1998.

claim: Neurocognition for all participant groups was assessed with the BACS.
source: Neurocognition for all participant groups was assessed with the Brief Assessment of Cognition in Schizophrenia (BACS) (Keefe et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about the assessment methods used, supported by citation to Keefe et al., 2004.

claim: The study was approved by the ethical committees of the Goethe University Frankfurt and the NHS Research Ethical Committee Glasgow and Greater Clyde.
source: The study was approved by the ethical committees of the Goethe University Frankfurt and the NHS Research Ethical Committee Glasgow and Greater Clyde.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent.
source: All participants provided written informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: CHR- and a matched control-group (CON1) were assessed at the Centre for Cognitive Neuroscience (CCNi), University of Glasgow.
source: CHR- and a matched control-group (CON1) were assessed at the Centre for Cognitive Neuroscience (CCNi), University of Glasgow.
evidence: This is a statement about data collection location.

claim: Five minutes, eyes-open resting-state was acquired using a 248-channel 4D-BTI magnetometer system at the University of Glasgow.
source: Five minutes, eyes-open resting-state was acquired using a 248-channel 4D-BTI magnetometer system (MAGNES 3600 WH, 4D-Neuroimaging, San Diego), recording at a sampling frequency of 1017.25 Hz, filtered online between DC and 400 Hz.
evidence: This is a statement about data acquisition methods.

claim: FEP- and chronic schizophrenia patients, and matched controls (CON2) were recorded at the Brain Imaging Centre (BIC), Goethe-University, Frankfurt, Germany.
source: FEP- and chronic ScZ-patients, and matched controls (CON2) were recorded at the Brain Imaging Centre (BIC), Goethe-University, Frankfurt, Germany.
evidence: This is a statement about data collection location.

claim: MEG resting-state activity for FEP and chronic schizophrenia patients was recorded with a 275-channel CTF system.
source: MEG resting-state activity was recorded with a 275-channel CTF system (Omega 2005, VSM MedTech Ltd., BC, Canada), recording at a sampling frequency of 600 Hz with a synthetic third order axial gradiometer configuration.
evidence: This is a statement about data acquisition methods.

claim: Online filtering was applied using a 4th order Butterworth filter with 0.5 Hz high-pass and 150 Hz low-pass for the CTF system.
source: Online filtering was applied using a 4th order Butterworth filter with 0.5 Hz high-pass and 150 Hz low-pass.
evidence: This is a statement about data acquisition methods.

claim: MEG data were analysed with MATLAB using the open-source Fieldtrip Toolbox.
source: MEG data were analysed with MATLAB using the open-source Fieldtrip Toolbox.
evidence: This is a statement about data analysis methods.

claim: Whole-brain source gamma-band power was estimated using the Dynamic Imaging of Coherence Sources (DICS) beamforming approach.
source: Whole-brain source gamma-band power (FFT data between 30 – 90 Hz, hanning tapered) was estimated using the Dynamic Imaging of Coherence Sources (DICS) beamforming approach (Gross et al., 2001) on a 5 mm grid based on the MNI template brain.
evidence: This is a statement about data analysis methods, supported by citation to Gross et al., 2001.

claim: Low and high-frequency bands have distinct generating mechanisms and functional roles.
source: We differentiated between a low (30 – 46 Hz) and high (64 – 90 Hz) gamma-band to avoid contamination of line-noise artifacts around 50/60 Hz, and because of evidence that low and high-frequency bands have distinct generating mechanisms and functional roles (Veit et al., 2017; Oke et al., 2010; van der Meer and Redish, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Veit et al., 2017; Oke et al., 2010; and van der Meer and Redish, 2009.

claim: Data were rescaled separately per trial and channel to values between 0 and 1 prior to source estimation and FFT computations.
source: Prior to source estimation as well as FFT computations, data were rescaled separately per trial and channel to values between 0 and 1 (formula: X(t) – minamp/(maxamp-minamp), with X(t) representing raw amplitude at time t, and minamp/maxamp estimated across time).
evidence: This is a statement about data preprocessing methods.

claim: The linear rescaling procedure was robust against changes in topographic distribution of activity and spectral power shifts.
source: Our tests showed that this linear rescaling procedure was robust against changes in topographic distribution of activity (including source estimations) and spectral power shifts.
evidence: This is a statement about the validation of the preprocessing method.

claim: The rescaling procedure was applied to correct for higher variance in overall brain activity levels in the FEP, schizophrenia patients and CHR participants, compared to healthy controls.
source: The procedure was applied to correct for (1) higher variance in overall brain activity levels in the FEP, ScZ patients and, to some extend also in the CHR participants, compared to healthy controls
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the preprocessing method.

claim: The rescaling procedure was applied to correct for MEG-system differences in global activity levels and sensor types.
source: and (2) MEG-system differences in global activity levels and sensor types (CTF gradiometers vs. 4D-BTI magnetometers).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the preprocessing method.

claim: MRS data were acquired on a Siemens Trio 3Tesla scanner and only for the CHR-group and their respective controls.
source: MRS data were acquired on a Siemens Trio 3Tesla scanner and only for the CHR-group and their respective controls.
evidence: This is a statement about data acquisition methods.

claim: A single 2 × 2 × 2 cm3 voxel was placed in the right middle occipital gyrus for MRS data acquisition.
source: The 3D MPRAGE anatomical images were first resliced into axial and coronal views to allow more precise and consistent placement of a single 2 × 2 × 2 cm3 voxel, using all three planar views, in the right middle occipital gyrus, about 1 cm to the right of the calcarine fissure and aligned within a few millimeters from the edge of voxel (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statement about data acquisition methods, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: FASTMAP shimming of the voxel was used to improve local-field homogeneity in the area of interest.
source: FASTMAP (Gruetter and Tkác, 2000) shimming of the voxel was used to improve local-field homogeneity in the area of interest.
evidence: This is a statement about data acquisition methods, supported by citation to Gruetter and Tkác, 2000.

claim: Metabolite quantification of the MEGA-PRESS difference spectra was performed using the Matlab Toolbox Gannet 2.1.
source: Metabolite quantification of the MEGA-PRESS difference spectra was performed using the Matlab Toolbox Gannet 2.1 (Edden et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about data analysis methods, supported by citation to Edden et al., 2014.

claim: GABA concentrations were adjusted for CSF contamination.
source: To account for individual differences in amounts of voxel gray matter (GM), white matter (WM) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fractions, GABA concentrations were adjusted for CSF contamination (contamination was on average ~1%).
evidence: This is a statement about data processing methods.

claim: GABA concentrations were corrected for the differences in water relaxation times of the different tissue types within the voxel.
source: GABA concentrations were additionally corrected for the differences in water relaxation times of the different tissue types within the voxel.
evidence: This is a statement about data processing methods.

claim: Both GABA and Glx concentrations were expressed as a ratio score using water (H2O) concentration as reference.
source: Finally, both GABA and Glx concentrations were expressed as a ratio score. Water (H2O) concentration (unsuppressed) was used as reference.
evidence: This is a statement about data processing methods.

claim: Group differences in whole brain gamma-band power were evaluated by a non-parametric Monte-Carlo permutation statistics in combination with independent t-tests and additional FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
source: Group differences in whole brain gamma-band power were evaluated by a non-parametric Monte-Carlo permutation statistics (using 2000 permutations) in combination with independent t-tests and additional False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical analysis methods.

claim: Significance was assumed for p-values<0.05 in the statistical analysis of MEG data.
source: Significance was assumed for p-values<0.05.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical analysis methods.

claim: Demographic and clinical variables were assessed with an independent sample Kruskal-Wallis tests, alpha-level 0.05 (two-sided), adjusted for ties.
source: Finally, demographic and clinical variables were assessed with an independent sample Kruskal-Wallis tests, alpha-level 0.05 (two-sided), adjusted for ties.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical analysis methods.

claim: BACS data were standardized (z-transformed) to a normative database, correcting for age and gender.
source: BACS data were standardized (z-transformed) to a normative database, correcting for age and gender (Keefe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about data processing methods, supported by citation to Keefe et al., 2008.

claim: Main GROUP effects for BACS data were followed up by pairwise comparisons, corrected for multiple comparisons using Least Square Differences (LSD).
source: Main GROUP effects for BACS data were followed up by pairwise comparisons, corrected for multiple comparisons using Least Square Differences (LSD).
evidence: This is a statement about statistical analysis methods.
